title: Circular arrangements
condition: Distinct objects on a circle; rotations are equivalent and reflections remain distinct.
prompt: Six physicists sit around a circular table. Three are mutual enemies and no two enemies may be adjacent. How many arrangements are possible, with rotations identified?

derivation.title: Begin with a row
derivation.text: Label every seat temporarily. The first seat has n choices, the next n−1, and so on.
derivation.diagram: Six labeled seats distinguish rotations.

derivation.title: Identify rotations
derivation.text: Each circular arrangement appears n times in the labeled-seat count, once for each possible position of a fixed person.
derivation.diagram: The same circular order rotates through the seats.

derivation.title: Fix an anchor
derivation.text: Equivalently, keep one person at the top and permute the others. No rotational duplication remains.
derivation.diagram: One seat becomes the fixed anchor.

derivation.title: Check the symmetry
derivation.text: Clockwise and counterclockwise orders generally differ. Divide by two only when the problem explicitly identifies reflections and no stabilizer changes the count.
derivation.diagram: The orientation is retained.

worked.title: Force alternation
worked.text: The three enemies need three separating friends. With only six people, enemies and friends must alternate.
worked.diagram: Enemy seats alternate with friend seats.

worked.title: Anchor a friend
worked.text: Fix Gauss at the top to remove rotations. Arrange the other two friends in the two remaining friend seats.
worked.diagram: Gauss is fixed; two friend seats remain.

worked.title: Place the enemies
worked.text: Each of the three enemy seats is separated from the others. All six permutations of the enemies now work.
worked.diagram: Three separated seats receive the enemies.

worked.title: Combine the choices
worked.text: The choices are independent, and the fixed anchor makes each arrangement unique.
worked.diagram: There are twelve circular arrangements.

trap: Dividing by six after already fixing an anchor removes the same rotational duplication twice.
check: Why must there be exactly one friend between consecutive enemies?
answer: There are three gaps between enemies and exactly three friends. Every gap must receive at least one friend, so each receives exactly one.

title: Stars, bars & upper bounds
condition: The variables are nonnegative integers; the bins are distinguishable. Upper bounds require extra work.
prompt: In how many ordered outcomes of five ordinary six-sided dice is the sum 24?

derivation.title: Encode a distribution
derivation.text: Write N stars in a row. Insert k−1 separators; the stars between successive separators give each variable.
derivation.diagram: Stars are separated into labeled bins.

derivation.title: Choose separator positions
derivation.text: Stars and bars occupy N+k−1 positions. Bars may be consecutive, representing an empty bin.
derivation.diagram: Separator positions become the objects being chosen.

derivation.title: Count the encodings
derivation.text: Choose the positions of the bars. Every nonnegative solution has one encoding and every encoding has one solution.
derivation.diagram: Every arrangement corresponds to one distribution.

derivation.title: Handle restrictions
derivation.text: Subtract lower bounds first. For upper bounds, subtract invalid encodings with inclusion–exclusion; stars and bars alone does not enforce them.
derivation.diagram: Shifting a lower bound frees the remaining stars.

worked.title: Count missing pips
worked.text: A total of 30 would mean all sixes. A total of 24 has six missing pips, with each deficit between zero and five.
worked.diagram: Six deficit stars are placed in five bins.

worked.title: Temporarily ignore the ceiling
worked.text: Count all nonnegative deficit vectors. These include vectors with a deficit of six, which would mean a die showing zero.
worked.diagram: Four separators among ten positions give 210 encodings.

worked.title: Remove impossible dice
worked.text: If one deficit is at least six, all six missing pips are on that die. There are five such vectors; two cannot occur together.
worked.diagram: The five all-in-one-bin cases are crossed out.

worked.title: Return to ordered outcomes
worked.text: Dice are distinguished by position, so each allowed vector corresponds to exactly one ordered roll.
worked.diagram: 205 legal outcomes remain.

trap: Using positive-variable stars and bars without the ceiling permits values greater than six.
check: Why are there no intersections between the five invalid events?
answer: Two deficits of at least six would sum to at least twelve, but the total deficit is only six.

title: Count the complement carefully
condition: A and B are finite sets in the same universe. Count their overlap once.
prompt: How many subsets of {1,2,…,10} have at most four even elements and at most two elements divisible by three?

derivation.title: Mark the two events
derivation.text: Counting each set separately counts points in their intersection twice.
derivation.diagram: Two overlapping regions are shaded.

derivation.title: Locate the duplication
derivation.text: Every element of the overlap received one count from A and a second count from B.
derivation.diagram: The overlap is highlighted.

derivation.title: Subtract one copy
derivation.text: Subtract the overlap exactly once. Every point in the union then has weight one.
derivation.diagram: The overlap carries one count.

derivation.title: Use a complement
derivation.text: When restrictions say “at most,” the violating events may be simpler to count than the allowed cases.
derivation.diagram: The region outside both events is retained.

worked.title: Describe the violations
worked.text: Let A contain all five even numbers and let B contain all three multiples of three. A valid subset belongs to neither event.
worked.diagram: The universe has 1024 subsets.

worked.title: Count each bad event
worked.text: Once the required elements are included, every remaining element may be present or absent.
worked.diagram: A has 32 subsets and B has 128.

worked.title: Count their overlap
worked.text: The required union is {2,3,4,6,8,9,10}. Only 1, 5, and 7 remain optional.
worked.diagram: The overlap has eight subsets.

worked.title: Restore the overlap
worked.text: Subsets violating both conditions were removed twice. Add one copy back.
worked.diagram: 872 subsets satisfy both restrictions.

trap: The required sets overlap at 6; there are seven forced elements in the intersection, not eight.
check: What changes if the two sets of forbidden requirements share no elements?
answer: Count the size of their union by adding their sizes. The number of optional elements is ten minus that union size.

title: Lattice paths through checkpoints
condition: Each step is one unit right or up. Ordered checkpoints must be coordinatewise reachable.
prompt: How many right/up paths from (0,0) to (5,6) avoid visiting all three of (1,2), (3,4), and (5,5)? Visiting one or two is allowed.

derivation.title: Encode the steps
derivation.text: A path is a word containing r right moves and u up moves. The order determines its geometry.
derivation.diagram: A path becomes an ordered sequence of steps.

derivation.title: Choose the right moves
derivation.text: Choose which r of the r+u positions contain R. The remaining positions must contain U.
derivation.diagram: Right-step positions are selected.

derivation.title: Split at a checkpoint
derivation.text: A path through (a,b) consists of an independently chosen prefix and suffix. Multiply their counts.
derivation.diagram: A marked checkpoint splits the path into two pieces.

derivation.title: Subtract the forbidden event
derivation.text: Distinguish “avoid every checkpoint” from “do not visit all checkpoints.” These are different events.
derivation.diagram: The forbidden family is isolated.

worked.title: Count every path
worked.text: Every complete path uses five right moves and six up moves.
worked.diagram: An eleven-step path reaches (5,6).

worked.title: Order the checkpoints
worked.text: Monotone paths visiting all three must visit them in this order.
worked.diagram: The three checkpoints appear along a monotone route.

worked.title: Multiply the segment counts
worked.text: The displacements are (1,2), (2,2), (2,1), and (0,1). Choose each segment independently.
worked.diagram: Four segments have counts 3, 6, 3, and 1.

worked.title: Exclude only that family
worked.text: Paths visiting fewer than three checkpoints remain allowed.
worked.diagram: 408 paths remain.

trap: Subtracting paths through each checkpoint separately answers the stronger, incorrect restriction.
check: Could a right/up path visit (3,4) before (1,2)?
answer: No. Both coordinates are nondecreasing, so a path cannot return to smaller coordinates.

title: Probability as an area ratio
condition: The joint distribution must be uniform over the sample region. Independence alone does not imply uniformity.
prompt: Alex and Bob independently arrive uniformly between 3 and 4 PM. Each waits fifteen minutes. What is the probability that they meet?

derivation.title: Choose two coordinates
derivation.text: Represent the two random choices by a point. First identify the region of possible pairs.
derivation.diagram: Two axes describe the choices.

derivation.title: Check uniform density
derivation.text: For independent uniform choices on intervals, equal-area subregions have equal probability.
derivation.diagram: Equal areas have equal probability.

derivation.title: Normalize
derivation.text: The whole sample region has probability one. Its area determines the density.
derivation.diagram: The whole sample square has probability one.

derivation.title: Translate the condition
derivation.text: An inequality becomes a region. Often its complementary triangles are easiest to measure.
derivation.diagram: A band is retained while corner triangles are removed.

worked.title: Measure minutes after three
worked.text: The square of side 60 represents all equally likely arrival pairs.
worked.diagram: The sample space is a 60-by-60 square.

worked.title: Draw the meeting condition
worked.text: They meet exactly when the later arrival is within fifteen minutes of the earlier one.
worked.diagram: A diagonal band has boundaries y=x±15.

worked.title: Measure the missed meetings
worked.text: The complement consists of two right triangles, each with legs 45.
worked.diagram: Two corner triangles each have legs 45.

worked.title: Take the area ratio
worked.text: The band occupies seven sixteenths of the square. Boundary points have probability zero.
worked.diagram: The meeting probability is 7/16.

trap: The waiting time is fifteen minutes on either side of the diagonal, not a fixed quarter of the square.
check: If the waiting time doubles to thirty minutes, what is the probability?
answer: The excluded triangles have legs thirty, so the probability is $1-30^2/60^2=3/4$.

title: Indicators & linearity
condition: Indicators take values zero or one. Linearity needs no independence between them.
prompt: A five-element subset of {1,2,…,30} is selected uniformly. What is the expected number of pairs of consecutive integers in it?

derivation.title: Count one feature
derivation.text: Replace a complicated total with simple yes/no contributions.
derivation.diagram: Each possible feature has its own indicator.

derivation.title: Compute its expectation
derivation.text: A zero-one variable has expectation equal to the probability it is one.
derivation.diagram: An active indicator contributes one.

derivation.title: Add the contributions
derivation.text: Choose indicators so that each object being counted contributes exactly once.
derivation.diagram: The total is the sum of the highlighted indicators.

derivation.title: Use linearity
derivation.text: Dependencies may complicate the distribution of X, but they do not prevent adding expectations.
derivation.diagram: Expectations add even for overlapping features.

worked.title: Index the adjacent pairs
worked.text: There are 29 possible consecutive pairs. An indicator records whether both members appear.
worked.diagram: The number line has 29 adjacent pairs.

worked.title: Count subsets containing a pair
worked.text: Fix the two members of one pair, then choose the other three numbers from the remaining 28.
worked.diagram: One fixed pair leaves three selections.

worked.title: Simplify the probability
worked.text: Equivalently, require the first specified number and then the second in a sample without replacement.
worked.diagram: Each pair has probability 20/870.

worked.title: Sum all indicators
worked.text: A run of three selected integers contributes two pairs, exactly as the question requires.
worked.diagram: The expected count is 2/3.

trap: Consecutive pairs overlap and their indicators are dependent. Independence is unnecessary here.
check: Does the subset {1,2,3,10,20} contribute one pair or two?
answer: Two: (1,2) and (2,3). Indicators count pairs, not runs.

title: Roots without solving for roots
condition: The roots of ax²+bx+c are counted with multiplicity; a is nonzero.
prompt: If r and s are the roots of $3x^2+6x-5=0$, find $r^3+s^3$.

derivation.title: Factor over the roots
derivation.text: The leading coefficient a must remain in front. This identity also holds for repeated or complex roots.
derivation.diagram: Two root factors are placed side by side.

derivation.title: Expand the product
derivation.text: The coefficient of x comes from choosing one root term, and the constant from choosing both.
derivation.diagram: The cross terms combine into the root sum.

derivation.title: Compare coefficients
derivation.text: Equal polynomials have equal coefficients. This reads symmetric information directly from the equation.
derivation.diagram: Coefficient pairs are aligned.

derivation.title: Build the desired expression
derivation.text: Expand the cube of the sum and remove the two mixed terms together.
derivation.diagram: The mixed cubic terms are canceled.

worked.title: Read the root data
worked.text: Divide coefficients by the leading coefficient 3 and keep the minus sign on the root sum.
worked.diagram: The root sum is −2 and product is −5/3.

worked.title: Avoid radicals
worked.text: The requested expression is symmetric, so finding each root separately adds unnecessary work.
worked.diagram: A cube expansion exposes the mixed terms.

worked.title: Substitute the two invariants
worked.text: The product term being subtracted is positive ten.
worked.diagram: The values −8 and 10 are aligned.

worked.title: Finish
worked.text: The answer depends only on the sum and product, not on a labeling of the roots.
worked.diagram: The symmetric result is −18.

trap: Forgetting to divide by a changes both the root sum and the root product.
check: What is $r^2+s^2$ for the same quadratic?

title: Reduce powers with an identity
condition: Polynomial division by x−a leaves a constant remainder. Other known polynomial relations can reduce higher powers too.
prompt: A real number x satisfies $x+1/x=\sqrt5$. Find $x^{11}-7x^7+x^3$.

derivation.title: Apply division
derivation.text: Dividing a polynomial by a linear factor leaves a remainder whose degree is less than one.
derivation.diagram: A polynomial is split into multiple plus remainder.

derivation.title: Evaluate at the root
derivation.text: Setting x=a makes the divisible part vanish.
derivation.diagram: The divisible part vanishes at x=a.

derivation.title: Use a known relation
derivation.text: More generally, reduce P modulo any polynomial g satisfied by x. At that x, the multiple of g vanishes.
derivation.diagram: A known zero factor can be discarded.

derivation.title: Seek structure first
derivation.text: Factor or group the requested expression before expanding large powers. The useful relation may be hidden by reciprocal terms.
derivation.diagram: The expression is regrouped around the known relation.

worked.title: Square the given relation
worked.text: Since x is nonzero, reciprocal powers are legitimate. Remove the middle term 2.
worked.diagram: The mixed term in the first square is removed.

worked.title: Square once more
worked.text: The same identity turns the sum of squares into a sum of fourth powers.
worked.diagram: A second squaring reveals the coefficient 7.

worked.title: Clear the negative powers
worked.text: Multiply by x⁴ and move all terms to one side.
worked.diagram: The reciprocal relation becomes a polynomial zero.

worked.title: Factor the requested expression
worked.text: Both possible real values of x satisfy the same zero factor, so no root choice is needed.
worked.diagram: The entire expression contains the zero factor.

trap: Squaring can introduce extraneous solutions when solving an equation. Here only consequences of an already given solution are used.
answer: The original expression contains 1/x, so x is already known to be nonzero.

title: Geometric sums by cancellation
condition: The finite formula requires r≠1; the infinite sum additionally requires |r|<1. At r=1 the finite sum is na.

derivation.title: Write the finite sum
derivation.text: Use a finite number of terms first so every cancellation is justified.
derivation.diagram: Successive terms form a geometric progression.

derivation.title: Shift by one term
derivation.text: Multiplication by r shifts each term into the position of its neighbor.
derivation.diagram: A shifted copy aligns matching terms.

derivation.title: Subtract
derivation.text: Every interior term cancels. Only the first term of the original and the last term of the shifted sum remain.
derivation.diagram: Only the two boundary terms remain.

derivation.title: Pass to a limit when allowed
derivation.text: The tail arⁿ tends to zero only under the convergence condition.
derivation.diagram: The final tail shrinks to zero.

worked.title: Write the two sums
worked.text: Both series converge because |a|<1. The opposite signs give conjugate denominators.
worked.diagram: Two complementary denominators appear.

worked.title: Use their product
worked.text: Multiplying removes the linear terms from the denominator.
worked.diagram: The product denominator is 1−a².

worked.title: Form their sum
worked.text: The same denominator appears, so solving for a itself is unnecessary.
worked.diagram: The numerator becomes 24.

worked.title: Compare directly
worked.text: The sum is one sixth of the given product. Both signs of a give the same answer.
worked.diagram: The sum is 336.

trap: A geometric series with r=−1 does not converge, even though 1−r is nonzero.
answer: Both sums equal 12. Their sum is 24 and their product is 144, still in the ratio one to six.

title: Telescoping to a Diophantine equation
condition: m and n are positive integers with m<n. Keep the first and last uncanceled terms.

derivation.title: Split one term
derivation.text: Put the right side over a common denominator. The numerator is (k+1)−k=1.
derivation.diagram: Each fraction splits into a positive and negative neighbor.

derivation.title: Write adjacent terms
derivation.text: The negative part of each term cancels the positive part of the next.
derivation.diagram: Neighboring fractions line up.

derivation.title: Cancel the interior
derivation.text: The last index is n−1, so the final negative denominator is n.
derivation.diagram: Only the first positive and last negative terms remain.

derivation.title: Check endpoints
derivation.text: A one-term sum reproduces the original fraction; this catches the common off-by-one error.
derivation.diagram: The endpoint check agrees with a single term.

worked.title: Collapse the sum
worked.text: The textbook expression has n−m terms, ending at n−1.
worked.diagram: All interior fractions cancel.

worked.title: Solve for the second endpoint
worked.text: Because n is positive, the denominator is positive and 1≤m≤28.
worked.diagram: The endpoint m lies below 29.

worked.title: Use divisibility
worked.text: The positive integer 29−m lies between 1 and 28 and divides 29². The only possibility is 1.
worked.diagram: The only admissible divisor is one.

worked.title: Recover the integers
worked.text: Check: 1/28−1/812=1/29. The pair meets both positivity and order restrictions.
worked.diagram: The valid endpoints are 28 and 812.

trap: Ending with −1/(n−1) loses the negative half of the last summand.
answer: That would give m=0, which is excluded. The other divisor 841 is also outside the permitted range.

title: Divisor sums from independent exponents
condition: The pᵢ are distinct primes and the aᵢ are nonnegative integers; divisors are positive.
prompt: Let $f(n)=\sigma(n)/n$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum of positive divisors of n. Find $f(768)-f(384)$.

derivation.title: Choose a prime exponent
derivation.text: A divisor of pᵃ can contain any exponent from zero through a.
derivation.diagram: Exponent choices are listed along an axis.

derivation.title: Combine distinct primes
derivation.text: Unique factorization makes these choices independent and produces every divisor once.
derivation.diagram: A grid combines two prime-exponent choices.

derivation.title: Distribute the product
derivation.text: Expanding the product chooses one prime power from each factor, so its terms are exactly the divisors.
derivation.diagram: Every grid point contributes one divisor.

derivation.title: Use geometric sums
derivation.text: Each finite geometric sum has ratio pᵢ. Since pᵢ is prime, pᵢ−1 is nonzero.
derivation.diagram: Geometric sums compact the divisor total.

worked.title: Factor the two inputs
worked.text: The inputs differ only by one factor of two, suggesting that most normalized divisor terms will cancel.
worked.diagram: The exponent grids differ by one column.

worked.title: Normalize before subtracting
worked.text: Dividing a divisor sum by n reverses the powers into reciprocals.
worked.diagram: Normalized sums align their shared terms.

worked.title: Cancel their common part
worked.text: All terms through 1/2⁷ cancel, leaving only the new last term.
worked.diagram: Only the extra eighth-power term remains.

worked.title: Simplify
worked.text: This avoids computing and subtracting two large divisor sums.
worked.diagram: The difference is 1/192.

trap: The divisor-sum function is multiplicative only for relatively prime factors.
check: Why is splitting 768 as 3·256 safe here?
answer: The factors are relatively prime. Their prime-exponent choices are disjoint, so every divisor has a unique decomposition.

title: Combine two congruences
formula: ax\equiv b\pmod m\ \Longrightarrow\ x\equiv a^{-1}b\pmod m
condition: A modular inverse a⁻¹ exists exactly when gcd(a,m)=1. Otherwise first check the common divisor.
prompt: Find the smallest integer greater than 100 that leaves remainder 5 on division by 9 and remainder 4 on division by 17.

derivation.title: Interpret a residue
derivation.text: A congruence describes an entire arithmetic progression, not one integer.
derivation.diagram: A residue class repeats around a modular clock.

derivation.title: Substitute into the second condition
derivation.text: Parameterize one condition exactly, then ask which values of k satisfy the other.
derivation.diagram: Each step of size m advances around the second clock.

derivation.title: Find an inverse
derivation.text: When m and n are coprime, Bézout’s identity gives an inverse of m modulo n.
derivation.diagram: A multiplying step reverses the residue advance.

derivation.title: Recover the progression
derivation.text: Translate back to x, then impose the requested size or sign condition.
derivation.diagram: The combined solutions repeat every mn.

worked.title: Encode the first remainder
worked.text: Every integer with remainder five modulo nine has this form.
worked.diagram: Start at residue five and advance by nine.

worked.title: Impose the second remainder
worked.text: Substitute the expression for N and subtract five.
worked.diagram: The target residue for 9k is sixteen.

worked.title: Invert nine
worked.text: Multiplication by two is valid because nine and seventeen are coprime.
worked.diagram: Multiplication by two finds k≡15.

worked.title: Select the first valid integer
worked.text: The preceding representative is −13. Direct checks give 140=9·15+5=17·8+4.
worked.diagram: The first representative above 100 is 140.

trap: Ordinary division is not automatically valid modulo m. It requires an invertible divisor or a careful reduction.
answer: Adding 9·17 preserves both remainders, and coprimality makes 153 the smallest positive common period.

title: Complete a product
condition: The identity is algebraic; integer solutions require integer factor pairs and all original restrictions.
prompt: A rectangular floor has integer side lengths $a<b$. A one-foot border occupies half the floor’s area. How many ordered pairs $(a,b)$ are possible?

derivation.title: Look for a missing corner
derivation.text: Three terms resemble the area of a larger rectangle missing one corner.
derivation.diagram: A rectangle is shown with one corner missing.

derivation.title: Add the corner
derivation.text: The needed corner has side lengths a and b. Add its area to both sides of an equation.
derivation.diagram: The missing corner slides into place.

derivation.title: Factor the completed rectangle
derivation.text: The new equation turns an additive relation into a product relation.
derivation.diagram: The complete rectangle factors into two side lengths.

derivation.title: Enumerate valid factors
derivation.text: An integer equation now becomes a finite factor search when the right side is nonzero. Check signs, order, and original geometry.
derivation.diagram: Factor pairs are matched to candidate dimensions.

worked.title: Write the painted area
worked.text: One foot is removed at each end of each dimension. The painted interior is the other half of the floor.
worked.diagram: The interior is inset one foot on every side.

worked.title: Complete the product
worked.text: Expand, double, rearrange, then add sixteen to form the product.
worked.diagram: The area equation becomes a product of shifted lengths.

worked.title: Check the signs and order
worked.text: A nonempty painted rectangle requires a,b>2. Negative factors could only both be −1, whose product is not eight. Order requires the smaller factor first.
worked.diagram: Only two positive factor pairs satisfy the order.

worked.title: Recover the dimensions
worked.text: The interiors have areas 30 and 24, exactly half the outer areas 60 and 48.
worked.diagram: Both candidate rectangles satisfy the area condition.

trap: A one-foot border shortens each interior dimension by two feet, not one.
check: Why is the factor pair (4,2) excluded?
answer: It gives a=8 and b=6, contradicting a<b. It is the same rectangle with the forbidden order.

title: Inradius, circumradius & coordinates
condition: A nondegenerate triangle has area K, semiperimeter s, inradius r, and circumradius R.
prompt: A triangle has side lengths 5, 12, and 13. Find the distance between its incenter and circumcenter.

derivation.title: Join the incenter to the vertices
derivation.text: The perpendicular distance from the incenter to every side is r. The three subtriangle areas add.
derivation.diagram: Three equal inradii form the heights of subtriangles.

derivation.title: Factor the common height
derivation.text: The half-perimeter appears naturally, giving r=K/s.
derivation.diagram: The three bases combine into the semiperimeter.

derivation.title: Relate a side to its chord
derivation.text: A chord subtending angle C at the circumference has length 2R sin C.
derivation.diagram: A side is a chord of the circumcircle.

derivation.title: Eliminate the sine
derivation.text: Combine the ordinary sine-area formula with the chord relation to obtain the circumradius formula.
derivation.diagram: The two area formulas identify the circumradius.

worked.title: Place the right triangle
worked.text: Since 5²+12²=13², the right angle can sit at the origin. The area is 30 and semiperimeter 15.
worked.diagram: A 5–12–13 right triangle is placed on the axes.

worked.title: Locate the incenter
worked.text: Tangency to both coordinate axes makes both coordinates of the incenter equal to r.
worked.diagram: The incircle has center (2,2) and radius 2.

worked.title: Locate the circumcenter
worked.text: In a right triangle, the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices.
worked.diagram: The circumcenter is the hypotenuse midpoint.

worked.title: Measure the distance
worked.text: Coordinates avoid constructing the angle between the two centers.
worked.diagram: The center-to-center segment has length √65/2.

trap: The incenter is generally not the centroid or the circumcenter; the centers must be located separately.
check: Can you check the result using Euler’s relation $OI^2=R(R-2r)$?
answer: $R=13/2$ and $r=2$ give $OI^2=(13/2)(5/2)=65/4$, agreeing with the coordinate result.

title: Signed area & an equal-area cut
condition: List the vertices of a simple polygon in boundary order and repeat the first vertex at the end.
prompt: A quadrilateral has vertices A=(0,0), B=(1,2), C=(3,3), D=(4,0). A line through A bisects its area and meets CD at (p/q,r/s), in lowest terms. Find p+q+r+s.

derivation.title: Use an oriented triangle
derivation.text: The determinant gives twice the signed area. Reversing orientation reverses its sign.
derivation.diagram: A triangle is measured by its signed cross product.

derivation.title: Sum around the boundary
derivation.text: Oriented triangles from the origin add; contributions outside the polygon cancel.
derivation.diagram: Boundary triangles add with orientation.

derivation.title: Close the polygon
derivation.text: The final edge back to the first vertex contributes too. Omitting it is safe only accidentally when that contribution is zero.
derivation.diagram: The last edge returns to the first vertex.

derivation.title: Take one absolute value
derivation.text: Sum signed terms first, then take the absolute value. Absolute values on individual terms destroy cancellation.
derivation.diagram: The final signed sum becomes ordinary area.

worked.title: Compute the whole area
worked.text: The cross products for A,B,C,D in boundary order sum to −15.
worked.diagram: The quadrilateral has area 15/2.

worked.title: Use the simple half
worked.text: The side AD lies on the x-axis, so the half-area triangle needs only the height of E.
worked.diagram: The cut isolates a triangle with base four.

worked.title: Find the height and position
worked.text: Set the triangle area equal to half the quadrilateral area, then use the line through C and D.
worked.diagram: The point E is where y=15/8 meets CD.

worked.title: Read the reduced coordinates
worked.text: Both fractions are already reduced and E lies between C and D.
worked.diagram: The requested numerator-denominator sum is 58.

trap: Taking absolute values before summing the signed cross products can overcount the polygon.
check: Why must E actually lie on the segment CD?
answer: Its x-coordinate 27/8 lies between 3 and 4, and its y-coordinate 15/8 lies between 0 and 3; it also satisfies the line equation.

title: An attainable bound with AM–GM
condition: All variables are nonnegative. Equality holds exactly when they are equal. Integer restrictions may prevent equality.
prompt: Nonnegative integers A,M,C satisfy A+M+C=12. Find the maximum of AMC+AM+MC+AC.

derivation.title: Start with a square
derivation.text: For nonnegative x and y, both square roots exist and every real square is nonnegative.
derivation.diagram: Two nonnegative lengths determine a square difference.

derivation.title: Rearrange
derivation.text: Expanding gives x+y−2√xy≥0. Equality occurs when √x=√y.
derivation.diagram: The unequal pair is compared with an equal pair.

derivation.title: Extend by equalizing pairs
derivation.text: With a fixed positive sum, replacing an unequal positive pair by their average increases its product. A maximizing positive tuple must therefore have all entries equal. Zero-product boundary cases cannot beat it.
derivation.diagram: Equalizing factors raises the product while preserving the sum.

derivation.title: Test attainability
derivation.text: A numerical bound becomes the maximum only if the equality configuration satisfies every original restriction.
derivation.diagram: All factors coincide at equality.

worked.title: Complete the product
worked.text: The extra terms are A+M+C+1=13, a fixed amount.
worked.diagram: The target is shifted into a product of three factors.

worked.title: Apply the fixed sum
worked.text: The shifted variables are positive and their sum is constant.
worked.diagram: Three positive factors have total fifteen.

worked.title: Bound the product
worked.text: AM–GM gives equality at A+1=M+1=C+1=5.
worked.diagram: The balanced factors are 5, 5, and 5.

worked.title: Check the original variables
worked.text: The equality case uses nonnegative integers with sum twelve, so the bound is attained.
worked.diagram: The maximum 112 is attained.

trap: Bounding AMC and AM+MC+AC separately is valid only if their equality cases are compatible.
check: Why is “at most 112” not a complete maximum proof?
answer: You must also produce an admissible triple attaining 112. Here (4,4,4) does so.

title: Change the base before comparing
condition: For real logarithms, a>0, b>0, and b≠1. Every variable base must satisfy these conditions.
prompt: For positive x with $x\ne1/3,1/2$, solve $\log_{3x}4=\log_{2x}8$. Write x=p/q in lowest terms and find p+q.

derivation.title: Return to the definition
derivation.text: A logarithm asks which exponent of b produces a.
derivation.diagram: The logarithm is rewritten as an exponent equation.

derivation.title: Take a common logarithm
derivation.text: The bases and arguments are positive, so taking natural logs is legitimate.
derivation.diagram: Both sides are measured with the same logarithm.

derivation.title: Bring down the exponent
derivation.text: The power rule follows from the exponential definition. The base cannot be one, so ln b is nonzero.
derivation.diagram: The unknown exponent becomes a linear multiplier.

derivation.title: Divide and retain the domain
derivation.text: A common base turns comparisons of unrelated logarithms into ordinary algebra.
derivation.diagram: The change-of-base ratio appears.

worked.title: Use one common base
worked.text: The excluded values ensure neither denominator is zero.
worked.diagram: The two logarithms share a numerator factor ln 2.

worked.title: Cross-multiply
worked.text: Cancel ln 2, which is nonzero, then cross-multiply the nonzero denominators.
worked.diagram: The equation becomes linear in ln x.

worked.title: Collect logarithms
worked.text: Expand the logarithms of products using x>0.
worked.diagram: The remaining logarithm is ln(4/27).

worked.title: Check and report
worked.text: The result is positive and different from 1/3 and 1/2. The fraction is reduced.
worked.diagram: The admissible solution gives 31.

trap: Canceling logarithms as if log(ab)=log(a)log(b) is invalid; products become sums.
check: Why were x=1/3 and x=1/2 excluded before the algebra?
answer: They make one of the logarithm bases equal to one, so the original expression is undefined.

title: Complex division & a rotation
condition: All four coefficients are real and c+di is nonzero. Multiplying by i rotates a complex number 90° counterclockwise.
prompt: A complex number z has imaginary part 164 and satisfies $z/(z+n)=4i$ for a positive integer n. Find n.

derivation.title: Use the conjugate
derivation.text: Multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate preserves the quotient and removes the imaginary denominator.
derivation.diagram: A vector and its reflection represent conjugates.

derivation.title: Compute the real denominator
derivation.text: Since i²=−1, the product is the squared modulus, positive for a nonzero denominator.
derivation.diagram: The denominator becomes a positive squared length.

derivation.title: Expand the numerator
derivation.text: Keep real and imaginary terms separate while expanding.
derivation.diagram: Real and imaginary components are collected.

derivation.title: Read a geometric operation
derivation.text: Multiplication by i sends (x,y) to (−y,x): a quarter-turn preserving length.
derivation.diagram: The vector turns ninety degrees counterclockwise.

worked.title: Name the real part
worked.text: The imaginary part is fixed, so only one real coordinate remains unknown.
worked.diagram: z lies on the horizontal line Im z=164.

worked.title: Clear the denominator
worked.text: The equality says z is a quarter-turn and fourfold dilation of z+n.
worked.diagram: The translated vector rotates and scales by four.

worked.title: Compare coordinates
worked.text: Equality of complex numbers requires equality of both real and imaginary parts.
worked.diagram: The real coordinate is fixed at −656.

worked.title: Solve and check
worked.text: Then z+n=41+164i is nonzero, and 4i(41+164i)=−656+164i=z.
worked.diagram: The shift n is 697.

trap: The imaginary part is the real coefficient 164, not the expression 164i.
check: What does multiplication by −i do geometrically?
answer: It rotates a vector ninety degrees clockwise and preserves its length.
